name: Lyndon B. Johnson
description: US president whose Great Society expanded civil rights and public services while his administration escalated the Vietnam War.

axes.brief: Voting-rights expansion and congressional legislation strengthened electoral inclusion.
axes.counter: Executive secrecy and surveillance of dissent qualified accountability.

axes.brief: Public-order policy and surveillance coexisted with civil-rights enforcement.
axes.counter: Support for equal rights is not automatically opposition to every coercive security measure.

axes.brief: Equal civic membership and minority recognition accompanied integration.
axes.counter: Integration and common institutions were still priorities.

axes.brief: The 1965 immigration reform replaced national-origin quotas with family and skill criteria.
axes.counter: Numerical limits and enforcement remained; abolition of racial quotas was not unlimited settlement.

axes.brief: Vietnam escalation and intervention in the Dominican Republic showed reliance on force.
axes.counter: Late negotiations and restricted bombing were substantial qualifications.

axes.brief: Alliances and international agreements coexisted with independent US intervention.
axes.counter: Treaty cooperation did not imply comprehensive international legal supremacy.

axes.brief: Public broadcasting, housing and health funding expanded within a private economy.
axes.counter: Medicare financing did not mean all medical facilities were publicly owned.

axes.brief: Kennedy Round liberalisation favoured international trade.
axes.counter: Agricultural protection and domestic procurement qualified unrestricted trade.

axes.brief: Private enterprise coexisted with wage floors, federal programmes and anti-poverty coordination.
axes.counter: Great Society services were not a routine command economy.

axes.brief: Anti-poverty support and opportunity were expanded without endorsing unrestricted guaranteed income.
axes.counter: Service provision and civil-rights opportunity differ from direct tax-and-transfer equalisation.

axes.brief: Civil constitutional government coexisted with public religious rhetoric.
axes.counter: Personal faith did not produce clerical control over legislation.

axes.brief: Civil-rights transformation and women’s opportunity coexisted with conventional family norms.
axes.counter: Later marriage-equality and reproductive policies cannot simply be attributed to this presidency.

axes.brief: Infrastructure, space and technical development were supported.
axes.counter: Conservation laws and modern medical uncertainties qualify simple development-first estimates.

axes.brief: Federal civil-rights and welfare standards limited resistant state policy.
axes.counter: States retained constitutions, ordinary policing and taxation.

axes.brief: Teaching experience and anti-poverty policy stressed deprivation and unequal opportunity.
axes.counter: A social explanation of disadvantage does not settle each inherited psychological comparison.
